2148.prule: No word stress. Dagbani is a tone language (two level tones, H and L, plus downstep; a possible falling tone in the Eastern dialect). The two reachable first-hand modern descriptions, both by native-speaker phonologists, deny stress outright: Inusah 2021 'Dagbanli like other Mabia languages is not stress marking... stress does not exist in the phonology of the language' (reporting Hudu 2007's duration/intensity measurements, which found no phonetic correlate for the syllables Olawsky called stressed), and Hudu 2022 'In a non-stress language like Dagbani' / 'the more prominent syllable does not bear stress'. Hudu 2022 posits a left-headed bimoraic (trochaic) foot inside the prosodic word on segmental/phonotactic evidence only, explicitly not stress.
2148.srule: Not mentioned in Inusah 2021 (ch. 5 'Suprasegmental phonology', pp. 155-158 and 192; literature review p. 29) or Hudu 2022 (pp. 272-274; sec. 3.2 pp. 287-288): both deny word stress of any degree ('Dagbanli like other Mabia languages is not stress marking'; 'a non-stress language like Dagbani'), so no secondary or rhythmic stress arises; Hudu 2022's left-headed bimoraic trochaic foot is diagnosed by segmental criteria and its head syllable 'does not bear stress'.

2149.tone: Two-tone system (HIGH/LOW) described as 'tone areas' rather than levels: High has zones rated 5/4, Low has 3/2/1 (norms 5 and 2); tone carries meaning ('Tone (and not stress) as a phonemic feature'), demonstrated by minimal tone pairs (à'kà 'ladder' vs à'ká 'road'; 'gúhè 'pine' vs gù'hè 'grass'). Stress is derivative of tone: first H syllable, else second syllable. Interactions: 1.4.a 'HIGH TONE WITH STRESS EXERTS AN INFLUENCE UP, on low tones'; 1.4.b 'STRESS ON LOW TONE SYLLABLE TENDS TO PUSH THE SYLLABLE UP IN THE LOW TONE AREA' (vè'lè eye-his may be ve2'le3 or ve2'le2 or ve2'le1); 1.2a utterance-final unstressed syllables lowered by intonation; 1.4.c glottal-closed syllables shorter, higher, 'more force'. The 1992 OPD (sec. 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)') says only 'Upper Asaro has two phonemic tones.' (àkà/àká, gúhè/gùhè) and 'Tone is not written.' -- does not discuss stress. The 1972 noun-inflection ms. (p.5 footnote): 'This is a tone language, but tone does not play a very significant part. There are only a few words which are identical except for tone.'

2152.dq: Stress is generally on the first syllable of the word.
2152.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.3 'Syllable Structure', p. 24, last sentence of the section, immediately before the heading '2.4 Morphophonemic Rules'; restated in sec. 2.5 'Consonant Gemination', p. 33. 2152.prule: Word stress on the first syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive, for all word lengths ('generally'); no conditioning on syllable weight, vowel length or morphology is stated.

Stress is generally on the first syllable of the word. ... Another possible explanation is that gemination only occurs in stressed syllables. Since stress, as mentioned earlier in section 2.3, occurs on initial syllables, the root final syllable in (52) is not stressed, and would therefore not be geminated. This solution however, does not apply everywhere as shown in examples (95) through (97) which have simple consonants following a stressed syllable. (95) [uke]…

2152.exq_: Stress is generally on the first syllable of the word.
2152.tone: The same chapter posits a preliminary two-tone system: sec. 2.2.2 'A preliminary study of tones suggests there are two tones: high (H) and low (L). The functional load for tone in nouns is very low; there are no minimal pairs for tone. There are only two patterns on two syllable nouns, namely all high or all low'; 'There are few high tone nouns.' Verbs with short root vowels fall into H-tone and L-tone classes ('H-tone verbs contain always begin with a H tone, while L-tone verbs begin with a L tone in most forms'); long-root-vowel verbs show three patterns all beginning with H; the L of the first syllable is replaced by H in 3rd-person present forms; automatic downstep noted ('H tone after an L tone has often been observed to be slightly lower than a preceding H'). Sec. 2.2.3: 'There are however, no minimal pairs differing only in tone, where length is the same and tone is different. That is, whenever there is a difference in tone there is also a difference in the segments.'... 'Tone will not be transcribed in the balance of this thesis.' Conclusion, ch. 6 Summary/Conclusions, p. 76: 'Further work must be done to determine how tone functions in the language'. The author never relates tone to stress; the stress statement is a separate, unargued sentence at the end of the syllable-structure section, and is used as a premise on p. 33 (initial syllable = stressed syllable) in an argument about gemination that the author then abandons ('At this point I cannot account for the...').

2153.tone: Sec. 3.2.1, p. 94: 'Darlong is a tonal language like other related Tibeto-Burman languages. As mentioned earlier, this analysis proposes that Darlong has two register tones: high tone and low tone.' Praat pitch tracks of minimal pairs (Figs 14-16), contrastive-pair table 15 (p. 96), tone-sandhi summary 3.2.3.4 (p. 97: 'L + H -> L H No change / L + L -> L L No change / H + H -> H H No change / H + H -> H L Final high becomes low'). Stress/accent is never treated as a category; a full-text search of every chapter finds 'stress' once (p. 92, the reduction remark) and 'accent' nowhere. Sec. 3.1.5.4 itself says smooth syllables 'can have all three tones', contradicting the two-tone analysis and suggesting the paragraph is adapted from a Daai Chin / Mon-Khmer template (So-Hartmann is in the bibliography). Darlong 1995 [1996] (ethnographic monograph, archive.org scan, p. 69) says 'There are three main tones - the upward, the downward and the level' and uses 'accent' only for the circumflex marking long vowels.

2154.heavy: Not weight-conditioned: Poppe 1930 p. 126 'всегда на первом слоге, хотя бы гласный его был и краток, а гласные всех последующих слогов долгие' (always on the first syllable, even if its vowel is short and the vowels of all following syllables are long). Vowel length affects only the non-phonemic pitch peak (Zhong 1982; Tsumagari's mora count).
2154.prule: Word stress (intensity peak, 強め / expiratory accent) falls on the first mora, i.e. the first syllable of the word (the first mora is always a syllable-initial (C)(S)V), regardless of syllable count or vowel length; Poppe 1930 p. 126 states explicitly that it stays on the first syllable even when that vowel is short and all following vowels are long. Non-contrastive (no oppositions), phonologically irrelevant per Tsumagari.
2154.srule: Not mentioned in Tsumagari 1985 §3.2 アクセント p. 237 (with fnn. 14-18) and English summary pp. 239-240: the only word-level prominences described are the first-mora stress and a separate non-phonemic pitch peak on the penultimate mora. Also not mentioned in Poppe 1930 §12, Poppe 1934 §9, Ōtake 2012 §2.2.4 or Yamada 2020 §1.3.3.5 (whose fig. 1-3 marks a single intensity peak, ●○○○○, in a 5-mora word).

2154.tone: Not a tone language. Tsumagari 1985 regards pitch rather than intensity as the main exponent of the (non-phonemic) accent: pitch peak on the penultimate mora, shifted to the preceding syllable-initial mora when the penult mora is a postvocalic V or coda C; fn. 17 (per reader): in short words the pitch peak can be masked by first-mora intensity. Tsumagari 2003 p. 135 (excerpt) and Engkebatu 1988 p. 150 / Ōtake 2012 fn. 10 (as reported) place the pitch on the last syllable; Ōtake 2012 (Hohhot-raised idiolect) marks pitch peaks mostly on the last syllable and says Chinese loans take the native pattern. All sources call the pitch non-distinctive.

2155.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Degema is described as a tone language with two tones, high and low, plus a downstepped high; 'accent' in the clitic test is operationalised as underlying lexical tone (full words have it, clitics do not), and every syllable of a phonological word carries a surface tone.
2155.quote: II. An Accentual Test Lack of independent accent has often been associated with clitics, whereas full words are considered as bearing accent. Degema clitics have no independent tone, i.e. underlying tone, unlike full words such as nouns, verbs, etc. However, they bear tone in the phonological word, since no syllable is toneless in such a word. Consider example (23): ... In the example above, the subject clitic that is toneless in (23a) bears a tone in (23b) as the verb forms a complex with it in the surface structure. ... NOTES (1) Degema has two tones — high and low, plus a downstepped high.…
2155.loc: p.184, sec. 'II. An Accentual Test' (incl. ex. 23 and the sentence after it); NOTES (1), p.190.
2155.idn: Usokun dialect of Degema (Glottolog usok1238, child of dege1246) (a named variety of the language)
2155.tone: Two-tone system (H, L) plus downstepped H (Kari 2002 note 1, p.190; same statement in Kari 2002 clitics-vs-affixes note 1 and Kari 2007 note 2). Rolle & Kari 2022 (lingbuzz/006614) p.2: 'Previous work has established two tones in Degema, high (H) and low (L), as well as surface downstepped high (ꜜH). Tone is lexically contrastive on nouns, adverbs, ideophones, and grammatical items (but not for verbs).' The string 'stress' does not occur in Rolle & Kari 2022 (a full-text search count 0) nor in Kari 2002 (words); 'accent'/'unaccented' is used only for lack of underlying tone (Kari 2002 affixes p.95: clitics and affixes are 'prosodically weak and therefore unaccented'). No source reached describes stress, metrical structure or a pitch-accent (culminative) system; this is a plain tone language with no stress statement.

2156.dloc: Vol. II, Ch. XXV, section 'Woordvorm en klemtoon', pp. 792-794 (stress passage pp. 792-793; stress shift with sentence rhythm and in contractions p. 794); footnote 1 p. 783 on stress marking in the wordlists; p. 779 for the 673-word count of the Dem list.
2156.prule: No fixed position. Disyllables: stress 'as a rule' on the penult in Dem (Le Roux says the tendency holds above all in Moni), with seven penult-stressed Dem examples (àmbò, bijěm, bela, kàbo, kalò, majoe, wobit) against ten Dem final-stressed counterexamples cited as 'examples of the reverse' (ali, àmbi, màboei, mědjà, měning, nèndèm, nasim, pani, oràk, tànè) and one stress-only minimal pair (àmà 'one' vs àmà 'mother'). Trisyllables: 'no fixed rule' -- in Dem now antepenultimate, now final; his own Dem examples on p. 793 are grouped under first-, second- and third-syllable stress (5, 11, 4 items), so all three positions occur. Compounds: main accent often penult 'but equally on all other syllables', no rule found. Stress is therefore marked per lexeme in the Dem-Dutch list (pp. 852-862; 673 words by Le Roux's own count, p. 779): stressed syllable printed roman, unstressed italic (fn. 1 p. 783: 'De klemtoon valt op de gewoon gedrukte lettergrepen').

2157.dq: Verbs based on the present stem are stressed on the personal endings; verbs based on the past stem are stressed on the last syllable of the stem, as in begoróm, “I take,” goróftom “I took,” bego-róftom “I was taking.” In compound verbs the incorporated nominal constituent is stressed. ... The past endings are enclitic and are identical with present-tense forms of “to be.”
2157.dloc: DEZFŪL iii, section 'Morphology' (noun-suffix paragraph: 'contrastive suffix, stressed -ka', 'deictive suffix, stressed -(h)a'; verbal-morphology paragraphs: 'unstressed modal prefix be-' through 'negated by the stressed prefix má-', including the stative sentence 'varsādám, varsādē´'); KHUZESTAN viii, section 'Morphology', numbered noun-marker list (1)-(6). Online articles, unpaginated.
2157.prule: Stress position is set by morpheme identity (stressed vs. unstressed affixes), stated morpheme by morpheme, never as a general word-level rule. Verbs: forms on the present stem are stressed on the personal ending (begoróm); forms on the past stem on the last syllable of the stem, the past endings being enclitic (goróftom, bego-róftom); the stative participle + ending likewise carries stress on the participle's last syllable (varsādám, varsādē´); the modal prefix be- and the prefix me- are unstressed; the negative prefix na- and the prohibitive má- are stressed; in compound verbs the incorporated nominal is stressed; the counterfactual suffix -ē is unstressed. Nouns: plural -(h)ā/-un, contrastive -(a)ka and deictic -(h)a are stressed; definite-object -(n)a, ezafe -e, indefinite and relative -i/-ē are unstressed enclitics. No statement is made about stress in bare (unsuffixed) noun stems.

2159.dloc: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.3 'Metrical Stress', p. 30; weight scale sec. 3.2.1 ex. (5), p. 26
2159.heavy: Sec. 3.2.1 ex. (5), p. 26: 'Light: (C)V /de/ 'two' /e/ 'that'; Heavy: (C)VC /ran/ 'gold' /us/ 'high'; (C)VV /hau/ 'rooster' /ā/ 'new'; (C)VVC /kīs/ 'saw' /ain/ 'school of fish''. Long vowels, the diphthongs /ai/ /au/, and coda consonants all make a syllable heavy; rule (11a) says 'heaviest', so (C)VVC outranks (C)VC/(C)VV by implication but no ranking is spelled out.
2159.prule: Primary stress falls on the heaviest syllable of the leftmost foot; if the leftmost foot has no heavy syllable, on the initial syllable. On Cain's examples this means: the first syllable if heavy, else the second syllable if heavy (/da'nī/ 'is going', /ma'tindā"bōṭu/ 'airplane'), else the first syllable (/'divehi/, /'aharen/ 'I'). Cain does not define the foot anywhere in the dissertation ('foot' occurs only in rule (11) and in glosses; moras are used — p. 26 'bimoraic', 'monomoraic', sec. 7.5.1 'three or more moras (at least two Light syllables or one heavy syllable)' — but never related to a foot), so the reading of the leftmost foot as the word-initial two-syllable window is an inference from the examples; a moraic-trochee footing gives the same outputs on them. Stress is non-contrastive.
2159.srule: Other heavy syllables in the word receive secondary stress if they are not adjacent to the primary-stressed syllable: /'aha"ren/ 'I', /ma'tindā"bōṭu/ 'airplane'. Nothing is said about secondary stress on light syllables.
2159.quote: Stress is not contrastive in Dhivehi, and is hard to determine. Intuitive judgments show that the Dhivehi stress rule is as follows: (11) a. Stress the heaviest syllable of the leftmost foot: /da'nī/ 'is going' b. If the leftmost foot has no heavy syllables, stress the initial syllable: /'divehi/, /'aharen/ 'I'. Thus, Dhivehi is a weight sensitive system very much like Sinhala (Letterman 1997: 236-247). Other heavy syllables in the word receive secondary stress (") if they are not adjacent to the primary stressed syllable ('): /'aha"ren/ 'I', /ma'tindā"bōṭu/ 'airplane'.

2161.prule: One culminative stress per phonological word, on that word's single heavy syllable; placement is lexical and unpredictable ('free stress') with stress-based segmental minimal pairs (Table 2.22: 'khü.nyüm 'supernatural being' vs khü.'nyüm 'rattle'; 'hâ.wa 'make sound' vs ha.'wa 'waste time, delay'; 'tâ.mẽ 'boar' vs ta.'mẽ 'be crazy'). Disyllables are either iambic (stress on the second/final syllable; 'much more common') or trochaic (stress on the initial syllable; minority, only the HF-M tonal pattern). Formal statement: 'Stress falls on the first heavy syllable from left to right', but weight is lexically determined and in trochaic words is itself diagnosed by the stress.
2161.srule: None: one stress per phonological word — 'a light syllable... attracts neither stress nor tone' (p. 63); in H.H trochaic words 'stress (and tone) will fall only on the initial syllable' (p. 67); the phonological word has 'maximally and minimally one heavy syllable or one foot' (p. 87). 2161.tone: Four tonemes (H, HF, L, M; Table 2.4 p. 62). One tone per phonological word, borne by the stressed heavy syllable; light syllables are toneless. tn.quote: Dimasa has a simple tone system. It consists of a three-way contrast which is high, mid and low. These are register tones and are lexical in nature. The high tone is marked as /ʹ/, the mid tone is marked as /ˉ/ and the low tone is marked as /ˋ/. These tones are limited to nouns, verbs, adjectives and some adverbs with free morphemes while the inflectional affixes do not carry tones except in cases of suffixation and tone sandhi. … Longer words, which are polysyllabic, carry lexical intonation in each syllable while tone is marked at the final syllable in Dimasa.

2164.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Stress (Druckakzent: unaccented / weakly / strongly accented syllables) is one feature in fixed tone-stress-length bundles ('prosodemes'); only 10 of 24 possible combinations occur, so the bundles, not stress, are the linguistic units. The two lexically distinctive prosodemes are anchored on stem syllables: DP I = class (1) high+strong+short with a following prosodeme-less syllable, (5) low+strong+short on monosyllabic stems; DP II = (8) falling+strong+long on polysyllabic stems, (7)/(1) on monosyllabic monemes. Rising and falling tones are always strongly stressed. The only position-by-count statement is the expressive prosodeme EP II = (1) (12) on the last syllable of a word or morpheme complex (intonational, not lexical stress).

2165.quote: Details of the stress patterns of Jaminjung and Ngaliwurru are unclear at present. Primary word stress generally falls on the first syllable of a phonological word. In canonical complex verbs, main stress falls on the coverb, at least when it precedes the verb; the verb receives secondary stress. 2166.heavy: Three grades. Light: a syllable ending in a short vowel; medium: a syllable ending in a long vowel, or ending in a short vowel checked by a single consonant; heavy: a syllable having a short vowel checked by two consonants, or a long vowel checked by one or two non-syllabic consonants. Short vowels = non-peripheral ɩ ʊ ə; long = peripheral i: e: ɛ: a: ɔ: o: u: (p. 43).

With one medium syllable preceded by one or two light syllables: stress unpredictable and phonemic (Rule III). Words longer than trisyllables split into two or more stress units (p. 70).
2166.prule: Weight-conditioned: three syllable grades (light CV-short; medium CV: or CVC-short; heavy CVCC-short or CV:C(C)). Rule I: the (unique) heavy syllable of a simple word is stressed, wherever it stands. Rule II: with no heavy syllable and two or more medium syllables, the last-but-one medium syllable is stressed. Rule III: in light(+light)+medium words (CəCV:, CəCəCV:) stress is unpredictable and phonemic.

Rule I: If there is one heavy syllable in the word, it is stressed. Two heavy syllables d…

2166.exq_: Stress in Dogri is predictable in some cases and unpredictable in others. [...] Rule III: When there is one medium syllable preceded by one or two light syllables, the stress is unpredictable and phonemic.
2166.tone: Dogri is a tone language with three word tones (level/even, high rising, falling-rising; 1980 p. 52; Ghai 1968 ARIPUC 2). pp. 60-61: 'In Dogri, which is a tone language, one cannot expect to find a consistent relation in pitch between stressed and unstressed syllables. But, as mentioned in 2.5, according to the auditory impression the position of tone in disyllabic words is determined by stress, so that the tone movement starts in the stressed syllable.' Sec. 2.5.3 (pp. 51-52) chooses stress over over-length as the phonemic property because stress determines the place of the word tone and enters the nasalization rules. Stress is thus a genuine, tone-independent category here, so not tone or pitch accent.

2170.dq: Given this definition, Drubea and Numèè can be classified as bona fide tonal languages: their word-prosodic system is entirely based on a lexical pitch-based contrast which has a morpheme as its domain – specifically the stem (and to a certain extent the verbal classifier prefixes, which get their register specification from a lexical tonal operation).
2170.dloc: §6.2 'Tone, register and the typology of word-prosodic systems', p. 40
2170.prule: No word stress is described. The word-prosodic system is a lexical register (tone) contrast: at most one underlying downstep per stem (Rivierre's marked 'low tone' vs unmarked 'high'), borne by a mora, in a lexically fixed but edge-independent position; many stems carry none. Disyllabic stems fall into three lexical classes /σσ/ 'forest', /ꜜσσ/ 'end', /σꜜσ/ 'crayfish' (ex. 34). The author tests and rejects an accentual (stress-accent) analysis: downstep is culminative but neither obligatory, syllable-dependent nor demarcative.

The latter are exclusively recent loanwords from French and English, in which the downstep is always in the initial syllable; that is, they all have the shape CVꜜV.CV(V). (§3.7 p. 27; a fourth lexical class confined to loans.) On cu…
2170.tone: Lionnet 2025 (building on Rivierre 1973 and Shintani & Païta 1990) analyses Drubea and Numèè as register-based tonal languages whose only underlying prosodic primitive is a lexical downstep (register feature l) on a mora of the stem, plus a postlexical epenthetic upstep (pre-downstep raising) and utterance-final raising (Drubea). §6.2 explicitly raises and rejects the hypothesis that the culminative downstep makes them accentual: it fails Hyman's (2006) obligatoriness and syllable-dependency criteria and is not demarcative (found on either syllable of disyllables). The article contains no statement about stress, intensity or non-tonal prominence (a full-text search of the whole text: 'stress' occurs only in the Hyman definition and in reference titles). Stems of >2 syllables: Rivierre hypothesised at most one downstep per stem, words with more being compounds (§3.8 pp. 27-28). Older sources agree the language is tonal without saying anything about stress: Gordon & Maddieson 1999 (Oceanic Linguistics 38: 66) 'is one of relatively few Austronesian languages that are tonal'; Académie des Langues Kanak Drubea page: 'il comprend deux tons distinctifs: un ton haut et un ton bas, ce dernier étant le ton marqué'.

2171.dq: im Dunganischen die Verteilung des dynamischen Akzents in den Komposita und in Wortgruppen im allgemeinen vom Ton abhängt (p. 39); the same rule is then illustrated on suffixed numerals (ji1gə, sы4gə), disyllabic compounds/words (mo4zы 'Mütze', fw1zы 'Brief'), and multi-word numeral groups 444/333/22/81 with bar-separated word groups (pp. 40-41).
2171.dloc: Section II, pp. 39-41: p. 39 general statement (tones + dynamic accent, accent placement depends on tone); p. 40 rule after the numeral table (tone 3/4 initial -> accent on sigma1; tone 1(2) initial -> accent on sigma2), fnn. 2-3; p. 41 non-numeral, tri- and quadrisyllabic compounds, fnn. 2-3 (Nebenakzent). Read from (Kramerius scans, Czech Academy of Sciences Digital Library) and the library.
2171.prule: Dungan has lexical tone and a dynamic (stress) accent whose placement is stated to be completely conditioned by tone, not by weight or syllable count: in a disyllable (root + suffix, or compound) the accent falls on the first syllable if that syllable bears tone 3 or 4 (type ˈσσ), and on the second syllable if the first bears tone 1 (2) (type σˈσ), even when the second syllable is a suffix (classifier -gə, nominal -zы, perfective -l'i). The same tone-driven principle governs three- and four-syllable compounds and numeral word groups (444 = ˈσσ|ˈσσ|ˈσσ vs 333 = σˈσ|σˈσ|σˈσ, where šы is the numeral 'ten' and bыj 'hundred').
2171.srule: Rhythmic secondary accent (Nebenakzent) stated only for longer compounds: in trisyllabic compounds of type σσˈσ (first syllable tone 1(2), e.g. numerals 11, 13, 70, 80) the first syllable often receives a Nebenakzent, avoiding two unaccented word-initial syllables; in four-syllable compounds of type σˈσ|ˈσσ (e.g. 82, 84) the second syllable's accent is weakened and the first syllable receives a Nebenakzent (clash avoidance). No secondary accent is described for other word shapes.

(p. 40) -- but note the hedge 'im allgemeinen' in the p. 39 statement, the bracketed yangping question (p. 40 fn. 2: 'Auf die Frage vom Vorhandensein des sog. zweiten Tons ... und von dem von ih…
2171.tone: Tone language: the source marks tones 1, (2), 3, 4 by superscript digits (p. 39 fn. 3) and explicitly asserts a dynamic accent alongside tone ('das Vorhandensein der Töne und des dynamischen Akzents'). Unlike Chinese, where accent is 'ein selbständiger, vom Ton unabhängiger Faktor', in Dungan accent placement is derivative of the first syllable's tone: tone 3/4 -> accent on sigma1; tone 1(2) -> accent on sigma2, even a suffix. The authors set aside whether a distinct 2nd (yangping) tone exists and how it affects accent (p. 40 fn. 2). Modern accounts (Salmi 2007 web text, sec. 1.2.3) analyse standard Dungan as 3 tones in isolation / 4 in connected speech with a neutral tone after tones 3 and 4 but a full rising tone after tone 1 -- the same asymmetry expressed tonally; they state no stress-placement rule.

2173.dq: The penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase is always lengthened. ... It is the locus of phrase-level stress (realized by vowel length alone) ... every phonological phrase has a single, obligatory foot covering the final two syllables.
2173.dloc: Volk 2011 sec. 1.6 (Phonological Outline) 'Phrase-Level Stress', p. 8; 'The Penult' p. 17; FHDT discussion p. 174; 'attraction to the penult' p. 188; Duruma corpus table (three speakers) and section 'Duruma: Competing Motivations' p. 31. Supporting: Volk 2013; Philippson 1998a; Philippson these.
2173.prule: Phrase-level penultimate stress only: the penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase is always lengthened, analysed as a single obligatory trochaic foot over the final two syllables of every phonological phrase; stress is realized by vowel length alone, pitch being reserved for the tone system. No word-level stress rule is stated; phrase-internal words carry no lengthened penult (Volk 2013 ex. 1: ni-na-mala ku-gula Ngu:wo). Stated for Mijikenda as a whole, Duruma explicitly included (three Duruma speakers in Volk 2011's corpus; Duruma forms ku-ha:dza / yu-na-ha:dza / yu-na-ri-ha:dza show length on the phrase penult).
2173.quote: [Volk 2011:8] Phrase-Level Stress The penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase is always lengthened. [p. 17] The penultimate syllable of a phrase enjoys special status in Mijikenda. It is the locus of phrase-level stress (realized by vowel length alone) and it is also the most prominent position for the expression of high tones, as we shall see repeatedly. [p. 174] As indicated above, the penult of the phonological phrase in Mijikenda is lengthened. This, I claim, is the only effect of phrase-level stress in the language, pitch naturally being reserved for the tone system. Penultimate …
2173.loc: Volk 2011 sec. 1.6 (Phonological Outline) 'Phrase-Level Stress', p. 8; 'The Penult' p. 17; FHDT discussion p. 174; 'attraction to the penult' p. 188; Duruma corpus table (three speakers) and section 'Duruma: Competing Motivations' p. 31. Supporting: Volk 2013; Philippson 1998a; Philippson these.
2173.idn: Mijikenda as a whole: 'a family of nine closely-related Bantu languages' (Chonyi, Digo, Duruma, Giryama, Jibana, Kambe, Kauma, Rabai, Ribe), all referred to as 'dialects' by convention; Duruma is explicitly one of the nine, with recordings of three Duruma speakers (Duruma1-3, questionnaire) and its own data sections…
2173.exq_: The penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase is always lengthened.
2173.tone: Duruma is tonal (privative /H/ vs toneless; Volk 2011, 2013). Underlying H shifts rightward within the phonological phrase ('High Tone Shift') and is heard on the penult, which Volk calls 'the most prominent position for the expression of high tones'; the phrase-final syllable is never high (Nonfinality); depressor consonants restrict the shift in Duruma (Volk 2011 sec. 'Duruma: Competing Motivations'; Volk 2013 ex. 8). Volk treats phrase-level stress as realized by length alone with 'pitch naturally being reserved for the tone system'. Philippson 1991 classes Mijikenda as 'a accent tonal' and says a foot 'ne peut etre entierement compris dans les limites d'un mot que s'il debute avant la more (structurelle) penultieme de ce mot' (these p. 484-485), a statement about the metrical foot for H attraction, not a stress rule; Philippson 1998a speaks of 'a strong demarcative stress on the penult syllable, often marked by lengthening before pause', compatible with Volk's phrase-level statement but not explicitly word-level.
